title: The Last Bus
text: Nadia checked her watch for the third time in as many minutes. The bus shelter was empty except for a crumpled newspaper that skittered across the pavement whenever the wind gusted. Above her, the streetlight flickered and buzzed like a trapped insect. The air smelt of wet stone, as if it might rain at any moment. It was almost half past nine, and the last bus to Wickford was already late.

She tugged her coat tighter and glanced at the small suitcase by her feet. Inside, wrapped carefully in tissue paper, was the birthday present she had spent three months saving for: a silver locket, engraved with her grandmother’s initials. Nadia had rehearsed her words all week, yet now they seemed to have deserted her.

At last, headlights swept around the corner and the bus wheezed to a halt. The doors folded open with a hiss. The driver, a stocky man with a bristling moustache, drummed his fingers on the steering wheel and peered at her over his glasses. “Where to, love?” he asked. “Wickford, please,” Nadia replied, her voice barely above a whisper.

She found a seat by the window and pressed her forehead against the cool glass. Street lamps blurred into streaks of amber as the bus rumbled through the sleeping town. The only other passengers, a sleepy man and a woman with a shopping trolley, barely looked up. Nadia thought about the locket again. She had washed cars, walked the neighbours’ dogs and sold her old books to save enough money. Her mum had warned her that the journey would be long and lonely, but Nadia had insisted. Nothing was going to spoil this surprise.

Halfway through the journey, the woman leaned across the aisle. “Visiting family?” she asked, not unkindly. Nadia hesitated. “My grandmother,” she said at last. “It’s her seventieth birthday tomorrow, and she thinks I’m at home revising for my exams.” The woman chuckled. “Then you’re in for a treat, love, and so is she.”

The bus shuddered to a stop in Wickford, and Nadia stepped down into the cold night air. The village was silent except for the distant hoot of an owl. She hauled her suitcase along a lane fringed with dripping hedges. Her feet ached, and the suitcase seemed heavier with every step. At last the cottage appeared, a single lamp glowing in its window like a beacon.

Nadia hesitated at the gate. What if her grandmother was already asleep? What if she was cross at being disturbed so late? Then the front door swung open, and there, silhouetted against the lamplight, stood her grandmother in her dressing gown, peering out into the darkness. “Nadia?” she whispered. “Is that really you?” Her voice trembled, and in the lamplight Nadia could see that her eyes were shining.

All the words Nadia had rehearsed so carefully evaporated once more, but this time it did not matter. She dropped her suitcase and ran. Behind them, the lamplight spilled across the path, warm and golden.

title: The Secret Gardener
text: Throughout June, Zara had studied the derelict plot behind Elm Court from her bedroom window, though she would never have admitted to being curious. For as long as she could remember it had been a wilderness of nettles and corroded wheelbarrow parts, and its guardian, the caretaker Mr Hendry, defended it with a ferocity out of all proportion to its worth. “Keep out,” he would growl whenever a football strayed over the fence. “That ground isn’t for children, and it isn’t for anybody.”

It was therefore a considerable surprise when, one Saturday, she noticed a row of green shoots pushing through the soil beside the shed. The nettles had been cut back, and someone had dug a neat trench and set bean canes into it, lashed together at the top like a small wigwam. By Sunday the earth was dark and damp, although not a drop of rain had fallen, and on Monday a scarecrow, fashioned from a broom and a moth-eaten cardigan, presided over the end of the row.

“Somebody’s been busy,” said her friend Tobi, peering through a gap in the fence. “Perhaps it’s a secret society.” “Or a ghost with a watering can,” Zara replied, only half joking. What troubled her was not who was responsible but why anyone would labour so carefully in secret, as if being seen might spoil something.

On Tuesday she set her alarm, packed a torch and a flask of squash, and settled behind the recycling bins. At half past five the sky was the colour of dishwater and even the pigeons had not yet begun to complain. Zara crouched with aching knees, watching the plot, while the only movement came from a snail crossing the path with enormous dignity.

She was on the point of abandoning her vigil when a door clicked and footsteps crunched across the gravel. A stooped figure in a flat cap rounded the corner of the flats, a full watering can in each hand. He set them down, knelt with a small grunt and began to loosen the soil around the beans with his bare fingers, as tenderly as if he were smoothing a child’s hair.

It was Mr Hendry. The man who bellowed at footballs was humming quietly to himself. Then Zara shifted her weight, a bin lid clanged, and he spun round, his face folding back into its habitual scowl. “You,” he said. “What possible reason have you for being out here at this hour?”
Zara stood up slowly. “I was looking for the gardener,” she said. “I think I’ve found him.”

For a moment neither of them spoke. Then the old man exhaled, and his shoulders slackened. “My wife’s at her sister’s until August,” he said gruffly. “She has grown beans on this plot every summer for forty years, but this spring her knees refused. I want it looking right when she comes home. Not a word to anyone.”
Zara grinned. “Can I help?” Mr Hendry regarded her for a long moment, then held out one of the watering cans. “Mind the shoots,” he said. “And next time your football comes over, knock first.”

title: Meerkats: Life in the Mob
text: Meerkats are slender, sociable mammals that inhabit the arid grasslands and semi-deserts of southern Africa. An adult weighs less than a kilogram and stands barely as tall as a school ruler, yet it is a remarkably resourceful animal. It is best known for its habit of rearing up on its hind legs, balanced by its tail like a tripod, to survey the landscape.

Meerkats live in cooperative groups called mobs, which typically number between twenty and fifty individuals. Each member contributes to the survival of the mob. Together they dig a large network of burrows with many entrances. These shelter them from the fierce midday heat and offer refuge whenever danger threatens. Because the food around a burrow eventually runs short, a mob may occupy several burrows in turn. After the chill of the desert night, its members gather outside each morning, warming their thinly furred bellies in the sun.

Since eagles, hawks, jackals and snakes all prey on meerkats, the mob cannot afford to forage carelessly. While most members search for food, one or more act as sentries, climbing onto a rock, a termite mound or a low bush to scan the sky and the ground. The dark patches of fur around a sentry’s eyes reduce the glare of the sun, rather like sunglasses. Sentries take turns, so that no individual goes hungry for long.

When a sentry detects a threat, it gives an alarm call, and the calls are far from identical. A sharp, urgent bark signals a bird of prey overhead, and the entire mob dives for cover at once. A lower, more drawn-out call indicates a predator on the ground, in which case the meerkats may gather to watch the intruder before withdrawing. Researchers have established that mob members respond differently to each type of call, which suggests that the sounds carry precise information. They are not simply cries of fear.

Foraging occupies most of the day. Meerkats possess an acute sense of smell and sharp hearing, allowing them to locate prey that other animals overlook. Their diet consists chiefly of insects, spiders and small lizards, although they also eat scorpions. Using long, curved claws, they scratch at the sand and dig out prey concealed beneath the surface. Adults also instruct their young: they bring pups scorpions whose stings have been removed, and with repeated practice the youngsters learn to handle live prey safely.

Newborn pups, whose eyes are shut at birth, remain in the burrow for their first three weeks. While the mothers are away foraging, other members of the mob take turns as babysitters. A babysitter guards the pups throughout the day and frequently forgoes breakfast in the process. Even meerkats that are not the pups’ parents share this responsibility.

Life in the desert is unforgiving, yet meerkats endure it through cooperation. Sentries keep watch, babysitters protect the young and adults teach the pups, so the survival of the mob depends on every member playing a part.

title: The Substitute
text: When Mr Abernathy-Clough marched into Class 5B on Monday morning, clutching a briefcase the size of a small suitcase and wearing a tie speckled with tiny penguins, twenty-eight children held their breath. Miss Baker had lost her voice, and all weekend a rumour had been racing along the corridor: substitute teachers could be tricked.

“It’s foolproof,” Dev had assured them in the cloakroom. “He doesn’t know any of us, so if we swap names, he’ll never get the register right.” Nobody had thought to ask what would happen if the scheme went wrong. Dev’s plans generally combined a great deal of enthusiasm with very little forethought.
“Good morning, Class 5B,” boomed Mr Abernathy-Clough, peering at the register through enormous spectacles. “When I read your name, please answer ‘present’. Amira Hussain?”
There was a pause. Then Callum, who was sitting at the front, raised his hand. “Present,” he squeaked, in what he believed was a convincing girl’s voice. Several children snorted into their sleeves.

Mr Abernathy-Clough blinked once, made a note and carried on. “Callum Reid?” At the back of the room, Amira lifted a hand and growled, “Present, sir,” as deeply as she could manage, which sounded like a frog with a head cold. Tobias had to bury his whole face in his lunchbox.

The rest of the register was a triumph, or so it seemed. Priya answered to “Dev”, Dev answered to “Priya”, and Ellis, who was exceptionally tall, answered to “Little Sam”, an achievement that very nearly ended in helpless giggling. Throughout, Mr Abernathy-Clough nodded gravely, as though children exchanged identities every day of the week.

“Splendid,” he said at last, closing the register with a snap. “A full house. Now, Priya, would you kindly distribute the books?” Dev leapt up and dashed round the room, delighted. “And Little Sam,” the teacher added, “please open the window. It has become rather warm in here.” Ellis, who had to duck beneath the light, obeyed.

All morning the substitute treated them precisely as they had asked. He praised “Callum’s” beautiful handwriting, which was really Amira’s. He invited “Amira” to read aloud, and Callum, who could not manage a sentence without stumbling, was obliged to trip his way through a page about Roman roads. By break time, the class was no longer certain who was fooling whom.

At lunchtime, Mr Abernathy-Clough tapped a folded sheet of paper on the desk. “I ought to confess,” he said, “that Miss Baker left me a seating plan. It has photographs.” The silence was so complete that they could hear the penguin tie rustling. “I have known exactly who you are since five to nine. However, I have not enjoyed a register so much in thirty years, and I would be sorry to have spoiled it.” He smiled. “Now, would the real Dev kindly tie his shoelaces before he trips over them?”

title: Raising the Iron Tower
text: On 31 March 1889, a small procession of officials began to climb the stairs of a tower that had not existed two years earlier. At its head was Gustave Eiffel, the engineer whose company had built it, and the climb was long and slow. At the summit, high above the rooftops of Paris, he raised the French flag. The tallest structure in the world was finished. More than two years of work had come to an end.

The tower had been designed for the World’s Fair of 1889, an enormous exhibition held in Paris to mark a hundred years since the French Revolution. The organisers wanted a spectacular entrance to the fairground, and a competition was held to find one. A plan for a tower of iron, taller than anything ever built, was prepared by engineers working for Eiffel’s company, and it was chosen. Work began in January 1887. Nobody knew whether such a tall tower of iron would stand firm, and many people watched the site with doubt.

Building the tower was less like ordinary construction than like assembling a gigantic puzzle. Nearly all of the pieces were made in Eiffel’s factory on the edge of Paris, where each one was cut and drilled with great accuracy. The tower needed about eighteen thousand separate iron parts, and every one had to fit its neighbours exactly. Carts then carried them to the site, where around three hundred workers joined them together with about two and a half million rivets.

The four enormous legs rose first, held steady by temporary scaffolding until a platform could join them at the first level. Once that was in place, the tower climbed faster, with cranes lifting each section into position. Many of the workers laboured at heights that would have unnerved most people, yet the whole project took just over two years, and it was ready in time for the opening of the fair. Visitors could now climb to the platforms and look out across the whole city.

Not everyone admired the result. Soon after work began, a group of well-known artists and writers published a letter protesting against what they called a useless and monstrous tower that would disfigure the city. Eiffel replied calmly and did not change his plans. He argued that the tower would have a beauty of its own, because its shape had been governed by the need to withstand the wind.

At about three hundred metres, the tower held the record as the tallest structure in the world until 1930. Its permit allowed it to stand for only twenty years, and it might have been taken down in 1909. But Eiffel had encouraged scientists to carry out experiments there, and its height made it ideal for a radio aerial. The tower proved so useful that the city let it stay, and it has since become the most recognisable landmark in France.

title: How a Vacuum Flask Works
text: A hot chocolate poured from a vacuum flask on a winter walk can still be steaming hours after it was made, and on a summer day the same flask can keep a drink pleasantly icy. This apparent feat of magic depends entirely on the way the flask is constructed and on the way heat behaves.

Heat always moves from a warmer place to a cooler one, and it does so by three distinct routes. In conduction, heat is passed through solid materials from particle to particle, which is why the handle of a metal spoon soon warms up in a hot mug. In convection, heat is carried by moving liquids or gases, as when warm air rises above a radiator. In radiation, heat travels as invisible rays, which is how the Sun’s warmth reaches us across empty space.

A vacuum flask is engineered to obstruct all three. It is essentially two containers, one nested inside the other and joined only at the neck. Almost all of the air has been pumped out of the gap between the inner and outer walls, leaving a vacuum: a space containing next to nothing. Since conduction and convection both depend on particles to pass heat along or carry it away, they are very nearly ruled out, and the two most important routes for heat to escape are blocked.

Radiation remains, because heat rays are able to cross empty space. To combat it, the surfaces facing the vacuum are coated with a thin, shiny layer, much like the silver on a mirror. This coating reflects the rays back towards the drink rather than allowing them to pass through, so a hot drink keeps its warmth. By the same principle, the coating turns heat from the outside away from a cold drink, which therefore stays cool.

The weakest point is the top, where heat could escape through the opening. A flask therefore has a tightly fitting stopper made of plastic or cork. These materials are poor conductors, and the stopper also traps the air above the drink, restricting convection. Every time the flask is opened, some heat is lost, so it is sensible to keep the lid on for as long as possible.

The vacuum flask was invented in 1892 by a Scottish scientist named James Dewar, who had no thought of picnics. He needed a means of storing extremely cold liquids for his experiments. Within a few years, others realised that the same design could keep drinks hot, and the idea spread around the world.

Even the finest flask cannot keep a drink hot indefinitely, because a little heat always escapes through the stopper and the neck. Nevertheless, by defeating every route that heat can take, the flask keeps hot things hot and cold things cold for many hours.

title: Agnes Pryce, Postwoman of Cwm Derwen
text: Agnes Pryce was born in 1893 in Cwm Derwen, a scattering of farms wedged into a steep Welsh valley where the nearest town lay eleven miles away, over a mountain pass. Her father was a shepherd and her mother a seamstress, and it was said that Agnes learned to read from the labels on her mother’s reels of thread. By the age of nine, she could recite every price in the village shop’s ledger, a talent the shopkeeper found impressive and faintly alarming.

When Agnes was seventeen, the valley’s postman retired, and nobody could be persuaded to replace him. The round covered twenty-two miles of rough track, crossing two rivers and a bog that had swallowed more than one boot. Agnes applied, to general astonishment. Told that a young woman could not possibly manage it, she promptly walked the entire route in a single afternoon, arriving back at the post office before closing time. She was given the job that evening.

For the next forty-nine years, Agnes carried far more than letters. The valley had no doctor’s surgery and no telephone, so she also carried messages, medicine and news. She learned which households would welcome a cup of tea and a chat, and which preferred a nod over the gate. In a battered notebook she recorded every family’s name and one thing she had noticed about them: a birthday, a lame sheepdog, a stubborn hip. A letter delivered by Agnes, people joked, arrived with a weather report and the latest local opinion attached.

Her most celebrated feat came in the winter of 1947, when heavy snow closed the pass for six weeks. Agnes refused to let the valley feel cut off. She built a sledge from an old farm gate and, dragging it behind her, delivered the post on foot as usual. She also organised the farms into a chain, so that a sack of flour or a bottle of medicine could be passed from door to door faster than any one person could carry it. Nobody was ever quite sure who had first suggested the idea, but everybody knew who had made it work.

In 1959, when a new road allowed the Post Office to send a van, Agnes retired at the age of sixty-six. The valley presented her with a clock, a bunch of flowers and, at her own request, a sturdy new pair of boots, which she promised to wear out. She did not rest for long. She turned the empty room behind the old post office into a lending library, filled with books donated by her neighbours. People came for the books, although, they admitted, they came mostly for the conversation.

The library stayed open for more than twenty years. Agnes’s notebook is now kept in a museum in the nearest town. Its final entry, written in her careful hand, consists of just two words: “All delivered.”

title: A Field Worth Keeping
text: Dear Councillor Hargreaves,

I am writing on behalf of the Willowbrook Residents’ Group to urge the council to reconsider its plan to sell Tanner’s Field for car parking. For eleven years, this field has stood unused at the end of Mill Lane, and I understand entirely why it looks like an opportunity. I would argue, however, that it is a far greater opportunity than a car park could ever be.

We propose to plant a community orchard: forty apple, pear and plum trees, with a mown path, a few benches and a small shed for tools. A young fruit tree begins to bear fruit within a few years, and after that it will feed a neighbourhood for generations. Every autumn, the fruit would be free to anyone who lives nearby, and any surplus could be shared with the food bank on Church Street.

The benefits reach well beyond the fruit itself. In spring, the blossom would give bees and other insects an early meal, while the branches would shelter birds all year round. On hot days, the trees would cast shade in a town that has too little of it. Most importantly, an orchard is a place where people meet. At present, a resident of Mill Lane may live beside a neighbour for years without exchanging more than a nod. Working alongside one another, we believe, would change that.

I anticipate your objection. Parking is a genuine problem, and the council’s budget is limited. But consider the costs. A car park would need to be surfaced, lit and drained at considerable expense, and it would serve only those who drive into the town centre for an hour or two. Our orchard would cost far less. A local nursery has offered the trees at a reduced price, and more than sixty volunteers, of all ages, have already promised to give up their weekends to plant and tend it. The primary school has even offered to help with the planting. I would also point out that the High Street car park regularly has empty spaces before noon.

Consider, too, the children of Willowbrook. Many of them have never seen fruit growing on a tree, and an orchard would become a living classroom in which they could watch the seasons turn, from the first blossom to the last apple. It would also offer a shaded bench and a gentle walk to older residents, who currently have nowhere to sit between the shops and the bus stop.
There is a further difference. A car park, once built, is unlikely ever to be undone. An orchard, by contrast, grows more valuable with every year that passes.
I would be delighted to show you the field and our plans in person. I hope you will give the residents of Willowbrook the chance to prove what we can do.
Yours sincerely,
Yasmin Farooqui
Chair, Willowbrook Residents’ Group

title: The Beech Wood in October
text: By the middle of October, the beech wood has stopped pretending to be green. The leaves, which in summer made a roof so dense that hardly a fern could grow beneath it, have turned the colour of copper pennies and toasted bread, and the whole wood glows as though lit from within. Walking beneath them, you feel less like a visitor than like someone who has stepped inside a lantern.

The trunks rise smooth and grey, unmarked by the deep furrows of oak or ash, like the legs of enormous elephants, and the air between them is cool, carrying the first faint bite of winter. High above, the branches spread in a lattice so fine that the sky appears in the gaps as pieces of a blue jigsaw. The light that filters down is low and slanting. It lays long bars of gold across the ground and turns each drifting leaf, for a moment, into a flake of fire.

Underfoot, the fallen leaves have gathered ankle-deep. They rustle, crackle and sigh at every step, and in the still air the sound carries far ahead of you, so that nothing in the wood can be surprised by your arrival. Beneath the top layer, the older leaves have darkened and softened into a damp brown blanket that smells of earth and mushrooms and rain. It is a smell that seems to hold the whole year inside it. Now and then a breeze combs through the canopy, and a shower of leaves spins down like slow, silent rain.

Everywhere there are signs of a wood preparing itself. Beech nuts, gathered in prickly cases the size of a thumbnail, lie scattered among the leaves, some split open to show their small, three-cornered seeds. A squirrel streaks up a trunk with a nut in its mouth, pausing halfway to scold the intruder before vanishing into the branches. Somewhere beyond, a wood pigeon clatters out of a tree, and the noise of its wings echoes for a long time. Far off, a jay gives one harsh cry, and the silence closes behind it like water.

On a rotting stump, a cluster of pale fungi has appeared overnight, their caps packed together like a crowd pressed against a window. Their sudden arrival is a reminder that the wood’s real work goes on out of sight, in the soil, where threads of fungus feed on fallen leaves and slowly turn them back into earth.

As the afternoon fades, the gold deepens to amber and the shadows lengthen between the trunks. A single leaf lets go of its twig and turns over and over on its way down, taking so long that you almost expect it to change its mind. It lands without a sound. The wood does not hurry, and after a while you find that you have stopped hurrying too.

title: How Light Carries Messages
text: Every time you watch a video or send a message to a friend on the other side of the world, the information may travel for part of its journey as flashes of light inside a strand of glass. These strands, known as optical fibres, are so thin that a single one is little wider than a human hair, yet together they form a network that stretches across continents and beneath the oceans.

An optical fibre has two main layers. At the centre is the core, a thread of exceptionally pure glass. Around it lies a second layer called the cladding, which is made from a different type of glass. A plastic coat covers the outside, protecting the delicate strand from scratches and from being bent too sharply. The crucial detail is that the two glasses are not identical: light travels a little more slowly through the core than through the cladding.

This difference is what keeps the light trapped. When a beam inside the core meets the boundary with the cladding at a shallow angle, it does not escape. Instead, it bounces back into the core, rather like a ball ricocheting off a wall. This effect is known as total internal reflection. The light zigzags along the fibre from side to side, and it can follow gentle bends and curves without leaking out.

To send a message, the information must first be turned into a code. A tiny laser or lamp at one end switches on and off many millions of times each second, producing pulses of light. A pattern of pulses can stand for letters, sounds or pictures, in much the same way that a pattern of dots and dashes can spell words in Morse code. At the far end, a detector notices the flashes and changes them back into the original message.

Fibres have several advantages over older copper cables. Light can carry far more information than electricity, so a single fibre can handle thousands of conversations at once. The signals are not disturbed by interference from nearby electrical equipment, and they weaken more slowly, which means they can travel much further before needing a boost. Even so, over very long distances the light gradually dims, so devices called amplifiers are placed along the cable at regular intervals to strengthen it.

Fibres also have drawbacks. Glass is brittle, so a cable must be handled with care, and a cable on the seabed can be damaged by a ship’s anchor, interrupting the messages it carries. Repairing a break demands skilled engineers, who must join the two tiny cores so precisely that no light leaks out at the join.

Despite these difficulties, a simple discovery about how light bends and bounces has become the invisible backbone of modern communication. Most of the time, we never notice it, which is exactly how the engineers would like it.

title: The Crows of New Caledonia
text: Among the forested islands of the South Pacific, New Caledonia is home to a bird whose behaviour has challenged an old belief. Scientists once thought that making tools was a talent confined to humans and their closest relatives. The New Caledonian crow, a glossy black bird with a heavy, straight beak, would scarcely earn a second glance on a woodland path. Yet how it finds its food has drawn researchers from around the world, who have spent decades watching, filming and testing it.

The crow’s principal prey is a plump grub that burrows into rotting timber, safely beyond the reach of even the longest beak. To extract it, the bird selects a slender twig and snaps it to a suitable length. It strips away the leaves and side shoots that would get in the way, pushes the twig into the tunnel and waits until the grub clamps its jaws on the tip. Then the crow draws out its meal. Some individuals refine the technique, breaking a twig off at a fork so that a small hook remains at one end, which they trim with meticulous care. Others tear strips from the serrated leaves of a pandanus plant, making narrow tools whose edges are lined with tiny barbs.

Perhaps more striking is the crows’ regard for their equipment. Individuals have been seen carrying a favoured tool from one feeding site to the next, rather than making a new one each time. Such conduct is rare, because it implies foresight: a bird that saves a tool for later seems to recognise that the object is worth keeping.

Tool-making is not an instinct that arrives fully formed. Young crows remain close to their parents for many months, and during that time they observe the adults at work with close attention. Youngsters can be seen handling twigs long before they are skilful, and it takes them a considerable time to master the craft. Biologists therefore regard the skill as largely learned rather than inherited.

A famous experiment at a university in Oxford showed how flexible this ability can be. Researchers placed a tiny bucket of food at the bottom of a narrow, upright tube and offered a crow a length of straight wire, which was useless for lifting the bucket by its handle. The bird wedged one end of the wire into a gap and tugged the other end with its beak until it bent, then hooked the bucket out. Because crows in the wild have no access to wire, the bird had not repeated a habit; it had solved a problem it had never met.

How much the crows truly comprehend remains contested. Some researchers argue that the birds reason about cause and effect, whereas others maintain that trial and error, together with a good memory, can account for the results. Whichever view eventually prevails, the crows have already forced scientists to reconsider what a small brain is capable of.

title: A Key in the Lining
text: The coat had hung on the rail for three weeks before Ines finally carried it to the till, a long bottle-green thing with cuffs rubbed thin and a faint smell of lavender and old paper. “Four pounds,” said the woman behind the counter, not lifting her eyes from a half-finished crossword. “Nobody else wanted it.” Ines, who was saving every spare coin for trainers and could scarcely afford a bus fare, paid anyway, without being able to say why.

It was on the bus home that her fingers, wandering idly along the hem, found something hard beneath a small tear in the lining: a brass key no longer than her thumb, knotted to a faded blue ribbon, with a card folded around it. The handwriting was so slanted and old-fashioned that she had to tilt the card towards the window to decipher it. “If you have found this,” it read, “ask at number 9, Coldharbour Lane.”

She read it four times and then rang the bell two stops early. Coldharbour Lane proved to be a narrow street of tall terraced houses whose doors had faded over the years to tired shades of red and green, and number 9, the last of them, had a crooked gate and lace at the window. Ines hesitated on the pavement, her imagination sprinting through every story she had ever read, before she pushed the gate open.

The door was opened by a small, upright woman with silver hair and a pencil tucked behind one ear, whose glance travelled from the coat to the key and back again as something in her face loosened. “Three weeks,” she said. “I had begun to fear that nobody was curious any more.”

Ines stared, for she had seen that pencil before, and that habit of tilting the head to one side. “You were at the till,” she said, “and you told me nobody else wanted it.” “And nobody did,” said the woman. “That was rather the point.”

She led Ines along a hall crowded with photographs of children squinting into the sun, each clutching a recorder or a trumpet, and into a front room where an upright piano stood beneath a knitted shawl, its lid shut. “I am Mrs Bhatt,” she said, “and this street was a good deal noisier in my time. These days my fingers ignore my instructions, and since the spring the piano has stayed closed. It is a poor thing for an instrument to be locked away with nobody to play it.” She nodded at the key. “I hoped someone might come and turn it.”
“So the coat was a trick,” said Ines, but Mrs Bhatt corrected her gently: “An invitation. A trick means I set out to fool you.”

Ines looked at the key, then at the piano, then at the key again, and found that the trainers she had been saving for mattered a little less than they had that morning. She knelt, fitted the key into the lock and turned it. The lid rose with a sigh, and the first note she pressed rang out through the room, low and true, as if the piano had been waiting for her all along.
